28.4  Subcycling (Mixed Time Integration) 
 
The time step size, ∆푡, is always limited by a single element in the ﬁnite element 
mesh.  The idea behind subcycling is to sort elements based on their step size into groups 
whose step size is some even multiple of the smallest element step size, 2(푛−1)∆푡, for inte-
ger values of 푛 greater than or equal to 1.  For example, in Figure 28.3 the mesh on the 
right because of the thin row of elements is three times more expensive than the mesh on 
the left. 

--- PAGE 633 ---
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
Time Integration 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
28-7 (Time Integration) 
 
Subcycling in LS-DYNA is based on the linear nodal interpolation partition subcycling 
algorithm of Belytschko, Yen, and Mullen [1979], and Belytschko [1980].  In their imple-
mentation, the steps are: 
1. 
Assign each node, 푖, a time step size, ∆푡푖, according to: 
∆푡푖= min (2 휔푗
⁄
) 
over all elements, 푗, connected to node 푖. 
2. 
Assign each element, 푗, a time step size, ∆푡푗, according to: 
∆푡푗 = min(∆푡푖) 
over all nodes, 푖, of element 푗 
3. 
Group elements into blocks by time step size for vectorization. 
 
 
In LS-DYNA we desire to use constant length vectors as much as possible even if 
it means updating the large elements incrementally with the small time step size.  We 
have found that doing this decreases costs with stability unaﬀected.

Hulbert and Hughes [1988] reviewed seven subcycling algorithms in which the 
partitioning is either node or element based.  The major diﬀerences within the two sub-
cycling methods lie in how elements along the interface between large and small elements 
are handled, a subject which is beyond the scope of this theoretical manual.  Nevertheless, 
they concluded that three of the methods, including the linear nodal interpolation 
method chosen for LS-DYNA, provide both stable and accurate solutions for the prob-
lems they studied.  However, there was some concern about the lack of stability and ac-
curacy proofs for any of these methods when applied to problems in structural 
mechanics.

In the timing study results in Table 1.1, ﬁfty solid elements were included in each

the case.  The eﬀect of subcycling for the more expensive fully integrated elements is 
greater as may be expected.  The overhead of subcycling for the case where 퐸1 = 퐸2 is 
relatively large.  This provides some insight into why a decrease in speed is often ob-
served when subcycling is active.  For subcycling to have a signiﬁcant eﬀect, the ratio of 
the major to minor time step size should be large and the number of elements having the 
minor step size should be small.  In crashworthiness applications the typical mesh is very 
well planned and generated to have uniform time step sizes; consequently, subcycling 
will probably give a net increase in costs.

The impact of the subcycling implementation in the software has a very signiﬁcant 
eﬀect on the internal structure.  The elements in LS-DYNA are now sorted three times 
• By element number in ascending order 
• By material number for large vector blocks 
• By connectivity to ensure disjointness for right hand side vectorization which is 
very important for eﬃciency. 
 
Sorting by ∆푡 interacts with the second and third sorts and can result in the creation 
of much smaller vector blocks and a higher cost per element time step.  During the sim-
ulation elements can continuously change in time step size and resorting may be required 
to maintain stability.  Consequently, we must check for this continuously.  Sorting cost, 
though not high when spread over the entire calculation, can become a factor that results 
in higher overall cost if done too frequently especially if the factor, 푚, is relatively small 
and the ratio of small to large elements is large.

A detailed discussion of the rigid body algorithm is presented by Benson and Hallquist 
[1986] and readers are referred to this publication for more information. 
29.1.1  Equations of Motion for the Body 
The equations of motion for a rigid body are given by 
푀휌풙̈ = 풇휌
푥,
(29.1)
푱휌흎̇ + 흎× 푱휌흎= 풇휌
휔,
(29.2)
where 푀휌 is the physical mass, 푱휌 is the physical inertia tensor, 풙 is the location of the center 
of mass, 흎 is the angular velocity of the body, and 풇휌
푥 and 풇휌
휔 are the forces and torques 
applied to the rigid body through *LOAD_RIGID_BODY. These are equations that can 
be found in a standard text book on rigid body mechanics.  The physical properties of a 
rigid body may come from three sources, these are 
 
1.Integration of the mass density 휌 over a region 푉 occupied by the rigid body, for 
which 푀휌= ∫휌푑푉, and  푱휌= ∫휌(풚−풙)⨂(풚−풙)푑푉. The initial rigid body coor-

∫휌풚푑푉
푀휌. Here 풚 is the integrand variable. 
2.Specifying properties using *PART_INERTIA, for which 푀휌, 푱휌 and initial coordi-
nate 풙 is simply speciﬁed in the keyword input deck. 
3.For a nodal rigid body, *CONSTRAINED_NODAL_RIGID_BODY, the physical 
properties vanish, i.e., 푀휌= 0 and 푱휌= ퟎ, and the position is arbitrary. 
 
Note that these are equations for the body itself, disregarding any interactions it may 
have with its surroundings.

for rotational updates of the inertia tensors) and can essentially be calculated at time zero.  
If mass scaling is active, the nodal masses and inertias include the added mass due to mass 
scaling and therefore change over time.  This means that inertia properties should be 
recomputed every time step to account for these changes, but the default behavior is that 
this is done only for nodal rigid bodies and not for regular rigid bodies.  Presumably this 
assumes that the inﬂuence from nodes is signiﬁcant for nodal rigid bodies and not so 
much for regular rigid bodies, which is probably true as long as the number of contiguous 
nodes is small compared to the total number of nodes in the rigid body.  Nevertheless, 
with RBSMS = 1 on *CONTROL_RIGID, these extra masses are accounted for and equa-
tions (29.19)-(29.24) are solved as expressed herein.  This amounts to transforming 풙 to 풛 
before the update, then update 풛, and transform back to obtain the new 풙.

The joint constraints are deﬁned in terms of the displacements of individual nodes.  
Regardless of whether the node belongs to a solid element or a structural element, only 
its translational degrees of freedom are used in the constraint equations. 
 
 
A spherical joint is deﬁned for nodes 푖 and 푗 by the three constraint equations, 
푥1푖−푥1푗= 0
푥2푖−푥2푗= 0
푥3푖−푥3푗= 0,
(29.59)
and a revolute joint, which requires ﬁve constraints, is deﬁned by two spherical joints, 
for a total of six constraint equations.  Since a penalty formulation is used, the redundancy 
in the joint constraint equations is unimportant.  A cylindrical joint is deﬁned by taking 
a revolute joint and eliminating the penalty forces along the direction deﬁned by the two 
spherical joints.  In a similar manner, a planar joint is deﬁned by eliminating the penalty 
forces that are perpendicular to the two spherical joints.  
 
 
The translational joint is a cylindrical joint that permits sliding along its axis, but 
not rotation.  An additional pair of nodes is required oﬀ the axis to supply the additional 
constraint.  The only force active between the extra nodes acts in the direction normal to 
the plane deﬁned by the three pairs of nodes. 
 
 
The universal joint is deﬁned by four nodes.  Let the nodes on one body be 푖 and 
푘, and the other body, 푗 and 푙.  Two of them, 푖 and 푗, are used to deﬁne a spherical joint for 
the ﬁrst three constraint equations.  The fourth constraint equation is,

(29.60)
and is diﬀerentiated to give the penalty forces 푓푛= −푘퐶∂퐶
∂푥푛, where 푛 ranges over the four 
nodes numbers.

29.3  Deformable to Rigid Material Switching 
 
Occasionally in practice, long duration, large rigid body motions arise that are pro-
hibitively expensive to simulate if the elements in the model are deformable.  Such a case 
could occur possibly in automotive rollover where the time duration of the rollover 
would dominate the cost relative to the post impact response that occurs much later.  
 
 
To permit such simulations to be eﬃciently handled a capability to switch a subset 
of materials from deformable to rigid and back to deformable is available.  In practice the 
suspension system and tires would remain deformable A ﬂag is set in the input to let LS-
DYNA know that all materials in the model have the potential to become rigid bodies 
sometime during the calculation.  When this ﬂag is set a cost penalty is incurred on vector 
machines since the blocking of materials in the element loops will be based on the part 
ID rather than the material type ID.  Normally this cost is insigniﬁcant relative to the cost 
reduction due to this unique feature. 
 
 
For rigid body switching to work properly the choice of the shell element formu-
lation is critical.  The Hughes-Liu elements cannot currently be used for two reasons.  
First, since these elements compute the strains from the rotations of the nodal ﬁber vec-
tors from one cycle to the next, the nodal ﬁber vectors should be updated with the rigid 
body motions and this is not done.  Secondly, the stresses are stored in the global system 
as opposed to the co-rotational system.  Therefore, the stresses would also need to be 
transformed with the rigid body motions or zeroed out.  The co-rotational elements of 
Belytschko and co-workers do not reference nodal ﬁbers for the strain computations and 
the stresses are stored in the co-rotational coordinate system which eliminates the need 
for the transformations; consequently, these elements can be safely used.  The membrane 
elements and airbag elements are closely related to the Belytschko shells and can be safely 
used with the switching options. 
 
 
The beam elements have nodal triads that are used to track the nodal rotations and 
to calculate the deformation displacements from one cycle to the next.  These nodal triads 
are updated every cycle with the rigid body rotations to prevent non-physical behavior 

--- PAGE 651 ---
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
Rigid Body Dynamics 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
29-13 (Rigid Body Dynamics) 
when the rigid body is switched back to deformable.  This applies to all beam element 
formulations in LS-DYNA.  The Belytschko beam formulations are preferred for the 
switching options for like the shell elements, the Hughes-Liu beams keep the stresses in 
the global system.  Truss elements like the membrane elements are trivially treated and 
pose no diﬃculties. 
 
 
The brick elements store the stresses in the global system and upon switching the 
rigid material to deformable the element stresses are zeroed to eliminate spurious behav-
ior. 
The implementation addresses many potential problems and has worked well in practice.  
The current restrictions can be eliminated if the need arises and anyway should pose no 
insurmountable problems.  We will continue to improve this capability if we ﬁnd that it 
is becoming a popular option. 
 
29.4  Rigid Body Welds 
 
The weld capability in LS-DYNA is based on rigid body dynamics.  Each weld is 
deﬁned by a set of nodal points which moves rigidly with six degrees of freedom until a 
failure criteria is satisﬁed.  Five weld options are implemented including: 
 
•Spot weld. 
•Fillet weld 
•Butt weld 
•Cross ﬁllet weld 
•General weld 
 
 
Welds can fail three ways: by ductile failure which is based on the eﬀective plastic 
strain, by brittle failure which is based on the force resultants acting on the rigid body 
weld, and by a failure time which is speciﬁed in the input.  When eﬀective plastic strain 
is used the weld fails when the nodal plastic strain exceeds the input value.  A least 
squares algorithm is used to generate the nodal values of plastic strains at the nodes from 
the element integration point values.  The plastic strain is integrated through the element 
and the average value is projected to the nodes with a least square ﬁt.  In the resultant 
based brittle failure the resultant forces and moments on each node of the weld are com-
puted.  These resultants are checked against a failure criterion which is expressed in terms 
of these resultants.  The forces may be averaged over a user speciﬁed number of time 
steps to eliminate breakage due to spurious noise.  After all nodes of a weld are released 
the rigid body is removed from the calculation. 

--- PAGE 652 ---
Rigid Body Dynamics

Contact-Impact Algorithm 
30.1  Introduction 
The treatment of sliding and impact along interfaces has always been an important capa-
bility in LS-DYNA and its predecessors.  We have implemented three distinct methods 
for handling contact: the kinematic constraint, penalty, and distributed parameter.  Of 
these, we use the ﬁrst approach for tying interfaces.  We discuss the relative merits of 
each approach in Sections 30.2, 30.3, and 30.4. 
 
Interfaces can be deﬁned in three dimensions by listing in arbitrary order all trian-
gular and quadrilateral segments that comprise each side of the interface.  We designate 
one side of the interface as the tracked side and the other as the reference side.  We refer 
to nodes on those surfaces as tracked and reference nodes, respectively.  In the symmetric 
penalty method, both sides of the interface act as the tracked and reference surfaces.  But 
for the other methods, LS-DYNA constrains the tracked nodes to slide on the reference 
surface after impact and remain on the reference surface until a tensile force develops 
between the node and the surface.  In the keyword input, surfaces A and B give the sur-
faces, where for nonsymmetric methods, A is the tracked surface and B is the reference 
surface.  
 
Today, automatic contact deﬁnitions are commonly used.  In this approach, LS-
DYNA internally generates the tracked and reference surfaces from the part IDs given for 
each surface.  For automotive crash models, including the entire vehicle in one single 
surface contact deﬁnition, where all the nodes and elements within the interface can in-
teract, is quite common. 
30.2  Kinematic Constraint Method 
The kinematic constraint method uses the impact and release conditions of Hughes et al.  
[1976].  It was initially implemented in DYNA2D [Hallquist 1976b] and extended to three 
dimensions in DYNA3D.  This method imposes constraints on the global equations by 
transforming the nodal displacement components of the tracked surface nodes along the 

--- PAGE 658 ---
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
30-2 (Contact-Impact Algorithm) 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
contact interface.  This transformation has the eﬀect of eliminating the normal degree of 
freedom of nodes.  To preserve the eﬃciency of the explicit time integration, the mass is 
lumped to the extent that only the global degrees of freedom of each reference surface 
node are coupled.  Impact and release conditions are imposed to ensure momentum con-
servation.  The release conditions are only of academic interest and were quickly removed 
from the original implementations. 
 
Problems arise with this method when the reference surface zoning is ﬁner than 
the tracked surface zoning as shown in two dimensions in Figure 30.1.  Here, certain ref-
erence surface nodes can penetrate through the tracked surface without resistance and 
create a kink in the slide line.  Such kinks are relatively common with this formulation, 
and, when interface pressures are high, these kinks occur whether one or more quadra-
ture points are used in the element integration.  It may be argued, of course, that better 
zoning would minimize such problems; but for many problems that are of interest, good 
zoning in the initial conﬁguration may be very poor zoning later.  Such is the case, for 
example, when gaseous products of a high-explosive gas expand against the surface of a 
structural member. 
30.3  Penalty Method 
The penalty method consists of placing normal interface springs between all penetrating 
nodes/segments and the reference segments.  The algorithm chosen dictates whether LS-
DYNA searches for segments penetrating segments or nodes penetrating segments.  The 
penalty method is available for both explicit and implicit contact methods.  Except for the 
spring stiﬀness matrix which must be assembled into the global stiﬀness matrix, the im-
plicit and explicit treatments are similar.  LS-DYNA calculates a penalty stiﬀness for each 
contact segment based on the element containing it.  A scaling factor for the stiﬀness in-
cluded in the keyword input controls the depth of penetration across the contact surface. 
 
Quite in contrast to the nodal constraint method, the penalty method approach 
excites little, if any, mesh hourglassing.  This lack of noise is undoubtedly attributable to 
the symmetry of the approach.  Momentum is exactly conserved without the necessity of 
Indicates nodes treated as free surface nodes
tracked surface
reference surface
Figure 30.1.  Nodes of the reference slide surface designated with an “x” are
treated as free surface nodes in the nodal constraint method. 

--- PAGE 659 ---
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
30-3 (Contact-Impact Algorithm) 
imposing impact and release conditions.  Furthermore, no special treatment of intersect-
ing interfaces is required, greatly simplifying the implementation. 
 
Currently, LS-DYNA has four implementations of the penalty algorithm:   
• Standard Penalty Formulation  
• Soft Constraint Penalty Formulation 
• Segment-to-Segment Penalty Formulation 
• Mortar Segment-to-Segment Penalty Formulation  
The standard penalty formulation is the default penalty formulation for all penalty con-
tacts other than Mortar contact.  It is speciﬁed by setting SOFT = 0 on Optional Card A. 
Setting SOFT = 1 and 2, respectively, in the input deck selects the soft constraint penalty 
formulation and segment-to-segment formulation.  To enable Mortar contact, use any 
contact type with MORTAR in the name.  SOFT is ignored in this case.  SOFT = 0 and 1 
search for nodes penetrating segments while SOFT = 2 and MORTAR look at segments 
penetrating segments. 
 
In the standard penalty formulation, the interface stiﬀness is chosen to be approx-
imately the same order of magnitude as the stiﬀness of the interface element normal to 
the interface.  Consequently, the computed time step size is unaﬀected by the existence 
of the interfaces.  However, if interface pressures become large, unacceptable penetration 
may occur.  By scaling up the stiﬀness and scaling down the time step size, we may still 
solve such problems using the penalty approach.  Since this increases the number of time 
steps and hence the cost, a sliding-only option has been implemented for treating explo-
sive-structure interaction problems thereby avoiding use of the penalty approach.  This 
latter option is based on a specialization of the third method described in Section 30.4. 
 
We implemented the soft constraint penalty formulation to treat contact between 
bodies with dissimilar material properties (such as steel-foam).  The stiﬀness calculation 
and its update during the simulation diﬀer from the standard penalty formulation.  The 
segment-to-segment penalty formulation is a powerful contact algorithm whose logic is 
a tracked segment-reference segment approach instead of a traditional tracked node-ref-
erence segment approach.  With this contact, the algorithm chooses which segment is the 
tracked segment and which is the reference segment unless a one-way contact type is 
chosen.  This contact has proven very useful for airbag self-contact during inﬂation and 
complex contact conditions.  Mortar contact is a diﬀerent kind of segment-to-segment 
contact suited for implicit analysis. 
 
Section 30.6 provides a more detailed discussion of the diﬀerent penalty methods 
other than Mortar contact.  We discuss Mortar contact in Section 30.23. 
30.4  Distributed Parameter Method 
This method was used in DYNA2D, and a specialization of it was the sliding-only option 
in DYNA3D.  In LS-DYNA, this method is used by 2D contacts with OPTION1 set to 
SLIDING_ONLY or SLIDING_VOID. For 3D contacts, this method is enabled by setting 

--- PAGE 660 ---
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
30-4 (Contact-Impact Algorithm) 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
OPTION1 to SLIDING_ONLY or SLIDING_ONLY_PENALTY. Motivation for this ap-
proach came from the TENSOR [Burton et.  al., 1982] and HEMP [Wilkins 1964] programs 
which displayed fewer mesh instabilities than DYNA2D with the nodal constraint algo-
rithm.  The ﬁrst DYNA2D implementation of this last algorithm is described in detail by 
Hallquist [1978].  Since this early publication, the method has been moderately improved, 
but the major ideas remain the same. 
 
In the distributed parameter formulation, half the mass of each tracked element in 
contact is distributed to the covered reference surface area.  The internal stress in each 
tracked element determines a pressure distribution for the reference surface area that re-
ceives the mass.  After completing this distribution of mass and pressure, we can update 
the acceleration of the reference surface.  Constraints are then imposed on tracked nodes’ 
accelerations and velocities to ensure their movement along the reference surface.  Unlike 
the ﬁnite diﬀerence hydro programs, we do not allow tracked nodes to penetrate; there-
fore, we avoid “put back on” logic.  In another simpliﬁcation, our calculation of the 
tracked element’s relative volume ignores any intrusion of the reference surfaces.  The 
HEMP and TENSOR codes consider the reference surface in this calculation.  For an out-
line of our sliding-only algorithm, see Section 30.15.

plied whenever a variable refers to either the tracked surface ∂b1, or reference surface, 
∂b2. Consequently, these superscripts are dropped in the development which follows. 
30.6  Sliding with Closure and Separation 
In this section, we will discuss all the penalty formulations speciﬁed with SOFT = 0, 1, 
and 2 on Optional Card A for 3D contact.  Section 30.23 discusses Mortar contact. 
30.6.1  Standard Penalty Formulation  
The standard penalty formulation is the default method for penalty contacts.  For 3D 
contact, it can be speciﬁed with SOFT = 0 (the default value) on Optional Card A. In ap-
plying this penalty method, each tracked node is checked for penetration through the 
reference surface.  If the tracked node does not penetrate, nothing is done.  If it does pen-
etrate, an interface force is applied between the tracked node and its contact point.  The 
magnitude of this force is proportional to the amount of penetration.  This may be 
thought of as the addition of an interface spring.

induce an instability when such scaling is performed.  If the soft material also has a low 
density, it may be necessary to reduce the scale factor on the computed stable time step.   
30.6.2  Soft Constraint Penalty Formulation 
Very soft materials have an undesired eﬀect on the contact stiﬀness, lowering its value 
and ultimately causing excessive penetration.  The Soft Constraint Penalty Formulation 
(SOFT = 1 on Optional Card A for 3D contact) gives an alternative to applying a scale 
factor on the contact stiﬀness for SOFT = 0.  The idea behind this option is to eliminate 
the excessive penetration by using a diﬀerent formulation for the contact stiﬀness.

30.7  Accounting for Shell Thickness 
Shell thickness eﬀects are important when modeling sheet metal with shell elements.  Un-
less thickness is considered in the contact, treating the eﬀect of thinning on the frictional 
interface stresses due to membrane stretching is diﬃcult. 
 
In the treatment of thickness for surface-to-surface and single surface contacts, we 
project both the tracked and reference surfaces based on the midsurface normal projec-
tion vectors as shown in Figure 30.3.  The surfaces, therefore, must be oﬀset by an amount 
equal to 1/2 their total thickness (Figure 30.4).  This allows LS-DYNA to check the node 
numbering of the segments automatically to ensure that the shells are properly oriented.  
Figure 30.4.  The tracked and reference surfaces must be oﬀset in the input by
half the total shell thickness.  This also allows the segments to be oriented auto-
matically.

Nodes-to-surface contacts treat the reference surface in the same way as the previously 
mentioned contacts.  These contacts project the tracked node in a direction normal to the 
contact surface with half the nodal thickness as shown in Figure 30.5. The nodal thickness 
is the maximum shell thickness over all the shells to which the node belongs. 
 
Single surface contacts, automatic nodes-to-surface, automatic surface-to-surface 
contacts, and constraint-based contacts always consider shell thickness oﬀsets.  Non-au-
tomatic surface-to-surface (including one way) and non-automatic nodes-to-surface con-
tacts do not by default account for shell thickness oﬀsets.  For these contacts, set SHLTHK 
to 1 or 2 on *CONTROL_CONTACT, or set THKOPT to 1 and SHLTHK to 1 or 2 on Op-
tional Card B to activate consideration of shell thickness oﬀsets.  SHLTHK = 1 excludes 
rigid bodies while SHLTHK = 2 does not. 
 
Thickness changes in the contact are accounted for if and only if the shell thickness 
change option is ﬂagged in the input (see ISTPD on *CONTROL_SHELL).  Single surface 
contacts additionally require THKCHG be set to 1 on *CONTROL_CONTACT to con-
sider thickness change.  Each cycle, LS-DYNA stores the nodal thicknesses while pro-
cessing the shell elements for use in the contact algorithms.  The interface stiﬀness may 
change with thickness depending on the input options used. 
30.8  Initial Interpenetrations 
The need to oﬀset contact surfaces to account for the thickness of the shell elements con-
tributes to initial interpenetrations.  These interpenetrations can lead to severe numerical 
problems when execution begins, so they should be corrected if LS-DYNA is to run suc-
cessfully.  Often an early growth of negative contact energy is one sign that initial inter-
penetrations exist.  Currently, LS-DYNA prints warning messages to the terminal, the 
d3hsp ﬁle, and the messag ﬁle to report interpenetrations of nodes through contact seg-
ments and the modiﬁcations to the geometry made by LS-DYNA to eliminate the inter-
penetrations.  Sometimes such corrections simply move the problem elsewhere since it is 
possible that the physical location of the shell midsurface and possibly the shell thickness 
are incorrect.  The single surface contact algorithms remove any nodes still interpenetrat-
ing on the second time step from the contact and print a warning message.   
 
For the automatic contacts, the IGNORE ﬂag speciﬁes the treatment of initial in-
terpenetrations.  The ﬂag can be set on Card 4 of *CONTROL_CONTACT, MPP1 of 
*CONTACT_OPTION, and Optional Card C of *CONTACT_OPTION. By default, LS-
DYNA moves the nodes to remove initial interpenetrations.  Changing the value of IG-
NORE causes LS-DYNA to track the initial interpenetrations but not eliminate them.  
With tracking, LS-DYNA applies a contact force if the penetration becomes larger than 
the initial interpenetration with a penetration depth equal to the diﬀerence between the 
two penetrations.  If the penetration becomes less than the initial interpenetration, the 
contact algorithms track this smaller penetration.  Thus, LS-DYNA ignores the initial in-
terpenetrations. 
 
For certain geometries, LS-DYNA cannot detect interpenetrations since the tracked 
node interpenetrates completely through the surface at the beginning of the calculation.  

--- PAGE 666 ---
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
LS-DYNA Theory Manual

master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
Figure 30.6 illustrates this type of undetectable penetration.  Another case contributing to 
initial undetected interpenetrations occurs when the edge of a shell element is on the sur-
face of a solid material as seen in Figure 30.7.  Currently, shell edges are rounded with a 
radius equal to one-half the shell thickness.  To avoid problems with initial interpenetra-
tions, consider the following recommendations: 
• Adequately oﬀset adjacent surfaces to account for part thickness during the mesh 
generation phase. 
• Use consistently reﬁned meshes on adjacent parts which have signiﬁcant curva-
tures. 
• Be very careful when deﬁning thickness on shell and beam section deﬁnitions --
especially for rigid bodies. 
• Scale back part thickness if necessary.  Scaling a 1.5 mm thickness to .75 mm 
should not cause problems but scaling to .075 mm might.  Alternatively, deﬁne a 
smaller contact thickness by part ID.  Warning: if the part is too thin, contact failure 
will probably occur. 
• Use spot welds instead of merged nodes to allow the shell midsurfaces to be oﬀset.

30.9  Finding Penetration by Tracked Nodes and Segments 
The original contact algorithms in LS-DYNA only performed an incremental tracked 
node search search.  This search ﬁnds for each tracked node its nearest point on the ref-
erence surface.  However this type of search fails when the tracked or reference surfaces 
are disjoint. Figure 30.8 illustrates such cases.  Many models extensively use tied inter-
faces creating what appears to the contact algorithms to be topologically disjoint regions.  
All of our algorithms other than a few older ones use bucket sorting algorithms to identify 
the contact pairs and incremental searching to track the position of the pairs between 
bucket sorts.  Note that non-automatic surface-to-surface including one way (*CON-
TACT_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE 
/ 
*CONTACT_ONE_WAY_SURFACE_TO_SUR-
FACE) and non-automatic nodes-to-surface (*CONTACT_NODES_TO_SURFACE) do 
not by default use bucket sorts if not accounting for shell thickness.  They only use incre-
mental searching.  Enabling accounting for shell thickness with SHLTHK = 1 or 2 causes 
these contact types to use bucket sorts with incremental searching like the other contacts.

The cost of the grouping operations, needed to form the buckets, is nearly linear 
with the number of nodes, 푁.  For typical LS-DYNA applications, the bucket sort is 100 
to 1000 times faster than the corresponding direct sort.  However, the sort is still an ex-
pensive part of the contact algorithms.  To further minimize this cost, the contact algo-
rithms perform the sort periodically and store the nearest three nodes.  Typically, bucket 
sorting absorbs three to ﬁve percent of the calculational costs when the contact deﬁnition 
includes most surface segments.  
 
For every contact in SMP and all segment-to-segment contacts in MPP and SMP, 
BSORT on Optional Card A sets the sorting frequency.  Depending on the contact type, 
the default bucket sort interval with BSORT is between 10 and 100 cycles.  BCKT on MPP1 
sets the sorting frequency in MPP for all contacts except segment-to-segment contacts.  
BCKT has a default value of 200. Except for high speed impact, the default interval is 
almost always adequate.  If nodes move from one disconnected surface to another in short 
time intervals or if the surface is folding onto itself, increase the contact bucket searching 
frequency, meaning reduce BSORT or increase BCKT. If two relatively smooth simply-
connected surfaces are moving across each other without folds, the bucket sorting can be 
performed at larger intervals.  Note that if the surfaces are more than several segment 
widths away from each other, no information is stored related to future contact, and later 
bucket searching is required to pick up future contacts.  Once a tracked node is in contact, 
incremental searching tracks the motion, and bucket sorting for the nodes, which are in 
contact, is not necessary.

nodes and rechecking these stored nodes every cycle to see if the nearest node changes, 
we avoid performing bucket sorting every cycle.  Typically, sorting every ﬁve to ﬁfteen 
cycles is adequate.  Implicit in this approach is the assumption that a node contacts just 
one surface.  For this reason the non-automatic single surface contact (*CONTACT_SIN-
GLE_SURFACE_... in LS-DYNA) does not apply to all problems.  For example, in metal 
forming applications contact often occurs on both surfaces of the workpiece.

encountered when moving in a direction normal to the surface away from 푘.  Figure 30.10

results into Equation (30.43).  This yields a cubic equation in 휂c.  
 
LS-DYNA solves Equations (30.42) and (30.43) numerically.  When two nodes of a 
bilinear quadrilateral are collapsed into a single node for a triangle, the Jacobian of the 
minimization problem is singular at the collapsed node.  Fortunately, there is an analyti-
cal solution for triangular segments since three points deﬁne a plane.  Newton-Raphson 
iteration is a natural choice for solving these simple nonlinear equations.  The method 
diverges with distorted elements unless the initial guess is accurate.  An exact contact 
point calculation is critical in post-buckling calculations to prevent the solution from 
wandering away from the desired buckling mode.

In concave regions, a tracked node may have isoparametric coordinates that lie 
outside of the [−1, +1] range for all reference segments, yet still have penetrated the sur-
face.  A simple strategy is used for handling this case, but it can fail.  The contact segment 
for each node is saved every time step.  If the tracked node contact point deﬁned in terms 
of the isoparametric coordinates of the segment, is just outside of the segment, and the 
node penetrated the isoparametric surface, and no other segment associated with the 
nearest neighbor satisﬁes the inequality test, then the contact point is assumed to occur 
on the edge of the segment.  In eﬀect, the deﬁnition of the reference segments is extended 
so that they overlap by a small amount.  In the hydrocode literature, this approach is 
similar to the slide line extensions used in two dimensions.  This simple procedure works 
well for most cases, but it can fail in situations involving sharp concave corners.

30.11  Contact Damping 
Viscous contact damping has been added to all contacts.  We originally intended it to 
damp out oscillations normal to the contact surfaces during metal forming operations.  
However, we later found it worked eﬀectively in removing high frequency noise in prob-
lems that involve impact.  The input requires a damping value as a percentage of critical, 
2푚, where 푚 is the mass and 휔 is the natural frequency.  Letting 푘 denote the interface 
stiﬀness, we compute the natural frequency for an interface tracked node from Equa-
tion (1.47). 
휔= √푘(푚tracked + 푚reference)

푚= min{푚tracked, 푚reference}.
(30.47)
The reference mass, 푚reference, is interpolated from the reference nodes of the segment 
containing the reference node using the basis functions evaluated at the contact point of 
the tracked node.   
 
Force oscillations often occur as curved surfaces undergo relative motion.  In these 
cases contact damping eliminates the high frequency content in the contact reaction forces 
but is unable to damp the lower frequency oscillations caused by nodes moving from 
segment to segment when a large angle change between the segments exists.  The hemi-
spherical punch deep drawing shown in Figure 30.16 gives an example of this phenome-
non.  The reaction forces with and without contact damping in Figure 30.17 show only 
minor diﬀerences since the oscillations do not come from the dynamic eﬀects of explicit 
integration.  However, reﬁning the mesh as shown in Figure 30.18 to include more ele-

30.13  Tied Interfaces 
Tied interfaces permit sudden transitions in zoning.  For instance, Figure 30.20 shows the 
joining of two meshes of solid elements.  This feature can often decrease the amount of 
eﬀort required to generate meshes since it reduces the need to match nodes across inter-
faces of merged parts.  With this feature, LS-DYNA ties tracked nodes within a certain 
tolerance of the reference surface to the reference segments.  For most tied interfaces, ty-
ing only occurs at the beginning of the simulation.  With oﬀsets enabled, the tied tracked 
node can be oﬀset from the reference segment.  Otherwise, the tied contact algorithms 
move the node to the surface during initialization. 
 
Since the contact algorithms impose the constraints only on the tracks nodes, we 
recommend making the more coarsely meshed side of the interface the reference surface.  

--- PAGE 681 ---
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
30-25 (Contact-Impact Algorithm) 
Ideally, each reference node should coincide with a tracked node to ensure complete dis-
placement compatibility along the interface, but in practice this is often diﬃcult if not 
impossible to achieve.  In other words, reference nodes that do not coincide with a tracked 
node can interpenetrate through the tracked surface. 
 
A key distinction among the diﬀerent types of tied contacts is whether they tie 
only translational degrees of freedom or tie both translational and rotational degrees of 
freedom.  Tying only translational degrees of freedom applies to elements that only have 
translational degrees of freedom.  Tying translational and rotational degrees of freedom 
applies to elements with rotational degrees of freedom like shells and beams.  
 
Most of our tied contacts enforce the tie with the kinematic constraint method (see 
Section 30.2). With some of the contacts, we enabled oﬀsets which switch the formulation 
from constraint-based to penalty-based (see Standard Penalty Formulation and Soft Con-
straint Penalty Formulation in Section 30.3). The penalty approach removes some major 
limitations of the constraint formulation: 
• Multiple tied interfaces can share common nodes. 
• Rigid body nodes can be constrained. 
• Tied interface nodes can have other constraints applied and can be subjected to 
prescribed motions. 
However, the penalty method does not enforce the constraint exactly. 
 
The keyword options OFFSET, BEAM_OFFSET, and CONSTRAINED_OFFSET 
enable oﬀsets.  The OFFSET and BEAM_OFFSET options change the tied contact from a 
kinematic constraint formulation to a penalty formulation.  Because they use penalty for-
mulations, they can be used for tying to rigid bodies.  We developed OFFSET prior to 
BEAM_OFFSET, so it suﬀers some drawbacks.  OFFSET uses discrete springs to transmit 
the force and moments while BEAM_OFFSET uses beam-like springs.  It does not couple 
Tied interface permits
mesh transitions

--- PAGE 682 ---
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
LS-DYNA Theory Manual

master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
moments and forces and thus does not enforce equilibrium.  Because of the type of spring 
model, OFFSET does not account for the moment associated with the oﬀset distance and 
can lead to nonphysical rotational constraints.  As an example, if we tie two oﬀset shells 
(with no boundary conditions applied) and apply an in-plane force to one of the shells, 
we would expect the system to rotate.  With OFFSET, no rotation occurs.  With BEAM_-
OFFSET or CONSTRAINED_OFFSET, the system rotates as expected.  
 
Some of the tied contact support failure.  Most of these include TIEBREAK in the 
name.  The TIEBREAK contacts speciﬁcally turn into sliding contacts after failure.  They 
are also penalty-based, so they can be used with rigid bodies.

30.13.1  Outline of Available Tied Contacts 
Here we will brieﬂy outline the tied contacts listed in Table 30.2.   
 
*CONTACT_TIED_NODES_TO_SURFACE and *CONTACT_TIED_SURFACE_-
TO_SURFACE should only be used for tying solid elements to solid elements because 
they do not constrain rotational degrees of freedom.  They may cause unrealistically soft 
behavior if used with shell elements.  These two contacts only diﬀer in input format for 
the tracked and reference surfaces.  The numerical treatment is the same.  They also can 
have the OFFSET keyword option.  These contacts work best if the surfaces are close since 
this oﬀset algorithm does not account for the moments associated with the oﬀset distance 
between the two surfaces as previously discussed.  *CONTACT_TIED_SURFACE_TO_-
SURFACE_FAILURE supports failure with failure stresses.  Segment oritentation is im-
portant to distinguish tension from compression for this contact. 
 
For shell-to-shell tying and beam-to-shell tying, use *CONTACT_TIED_SHELL_-
EDGE_TO_SURFACE as it includes tying of rotational degrees of freedom.  The tied in-
terface allows tying of edges of shells to shell surfaces (see Figure 30.22).  In such 
transitions the contact algorithm does not consider shell thickness.  Note that for implicit, 
setting IACC = 1 enables using the oﬀset versions of either *CONTACT_TIED_NODES_-
TO_SURFACE or *CONTACT_TIED_SHELL_EDGE_TO_SURFACE with any type of el-
ement.  The contact algorithms apply the rotational constraints automatically as needed 
(see Section 30.14). 

--- PAGE 684 ---
Contact-Impact Algorithm

master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
 
For modeling beam spot welds, use *CONTACT_SPOTWELD or *CONTACT_-
SPOTWELD_WITH_TORSION (see Figure 30.23). The beams are the tracked surface 
while the shell surfaces are the reference.  With the TORSION option, the contact algo-
rithm transmits the torsional forces in the beam as equivalent forces to the surrounding 
nodes of the reference surface.  The rotational constraint about the axis of the beam is 
then enforced.  The nonlinear shell elements in LS-DYNA have a zero stiﬀness drilling 
degree of freedom at each node, so it is necessary to carry the torsional forces through the 
membrane behavior of the shell. 
 
We developed *CONTACT_TIED_SHELL_EDGE_TO_SOLID for tying shells or 
beams to solids.  This tied contact transfers moments from shells to solids through forces.

30.13.2  Implementation of Constraint-Based Tied Contacts 
The implementation of tied interface constraints is straightforward.  Each time step we 
loop through the tied interfaces and update each one independently.  First, we distribute 
the nodal forces and nodal mass of each tracked node to the reference nodes, which deﬁne 
the segment containing the contact point.  In other words, we add the increments in mass 
and forces 
∆푓푟
푖= 휙푖(휉푐,휂푐)푓푡
(30.56)
to the mass and force vector of the reference surface.  After the summation over all 
tracked nodes is complete, we can compute the acceleration of the reference surface.  The 
acceleration of each tracked node 푎푖푡 is then interpolated from the reference segment con-
taining its contact points: 
푎푖푡= ∑휙푗(휉푐, 휂푐)푎푖
푗
4
푗=1
.
(30.57)
Velocities and displacements are now updated normally. 
 
The interpolated contact point, (휉푐, 휂푐), for each tracked node is computed once 
since its relative position on the reference segment is constant for the duration of the cal-
culation.  If the closest point projection of the tracked node to the reference surface is non-
orthogonal, values of (휉푐, 휂푐) greater than unity will be computed.  To allow for slight 
errors in the mesh deﬁnition, the tracked node is left unconstrained if the magnitude of 
the contact point exceeds 1.02.  Great care should be exercised in setting up tied interfaces 
to ensure that the tracked nodes are covered by reference segments. 
 
Conﬂicting constraints must be avoided.  Care should be taken not to include 
nodes that are involved in a tied interfaces in another tied interface, in constraint sets 
such as nodal constraint sets, in linear constraint equations, and in spot welds.  Further-
more, constraint-based tied interfaces between rigid and deformable bodies are not per-
mitted.  LS-DYNA checks for conﬂicting constraints on nodal points and if such conﬂicts 
are found, the calculation terminates with an error message identifying the conﬂict.  
Nodes in tied interfaces should not be included as tracked nodes in rigid wall deﬁnitions 
since interactions with stonewalls cause the constraints that were applied in the tied in-
terface logic to be violated.  We do not currently check for this latter condition is 
LS-DYNA.  
 
Tied interfaces require coincident surfaces.  For shell elements, this requirement 
means that the midsurfaces must be coincident.  Consider Figure 30.24 where identical

LS-DYNA projects tied tracked nodes back to the reference surface if possible and 
prints warning messages for all projected oﬀset nodes or nodes too far away to tie.  This 
projection eliminates the problems with rotational constraints but creates other diﬃcul-
ties: 
• Geometry is modiﬁed. 
• Tied interfaces must be excluded from automatic generation since tied surfaces 
cannot be mixed with automatic contact with thickness oﬀsets. 
30.13.3  Tiebreak Contacts 
Tiebreak contacts model connections that transmit both compressive and tensile forces 
with optional failure.  For instance, they can model glue.  These contacts are all penalty-
based.  Thus, tracked and reference nodes in a tiebreak contact can belong to other con-
straints and can belong to rigid bodies.  No sliding is allowed between the elements used 
in the tiebreak deﬁnitions until failure.  Upon failure, most of these contacts turn into 
regular sliding contacts.  The failure criteria depends on the contact type and can be based 
on stress or force. 
 
The older tiebreak contacts are non-automatic.  These contacts are TIEBREAK_-
NODES_ONLY, TIEBREAK_NODES_TO_SURFACE, TIEBREAK_SURFACE_TO_SUR-
FACE, and TIEBREAK_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE_ONLY. Because they are non-
automatic, segment orientation is important for determining the tensile and compressive 
directions.  They all only tie nodes at the beginning of the simulation.  The TIEBREAK_-
NODES_ONLY and TIEBREAK_NODES_TO_SURFACE are the same contact until fail-
ure.  They fail with following force-based criterion:

thickness oﬀsets, set THKOFF = 1 on Card 4 of the contact deﬁnition. 
 
The options for automatic tiebreak are: 
AUTOMATIC_GENERAL_TIEBREAK 
AUTOMATIC_ONE_WAY_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE_TIEBREAK 
AUTOMATIC_ONE_WAY_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE_TIEBREAK_DAMPING 
AUTOMATIC_SINGLE_SURFACE_TIEBREAK 
AUTOMATIC_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE_TIEBREAK 
AUTOMATIC_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE_TIEBREAK_MORTAR 
AUTOMATIC_ONE_WAY_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE_TIEBREAK_USER 
AUTOMATIC_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE_TIEBREAK_USER 
AUTOMATIC_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE_TIEBREAK_USER_MORTAR 
 
After failure, all of these contacts act as normal sliding contacts with thickness oﬀsets.  
Since they are automatic, LS-DYNA automatically orients the shell/segment normals.  
They all fail with a stress-based failure model.  The failure model for the non-USER ver-
sions depends on OPTION on Card 4. OPTION also determines when LS-DYNA ties 
tracked nodes to the reference surface.  With some choices of OPTION, tying can occur 
throughout the simulation instead of at the beginning of the simulation.  OPTION also 
determines the kinds of elements that can be tied and whether the contact transfers mo-
ments.  Some OPTION choices also enable damage modeling.  With the USER versions, 
you provide the failure model and damage model in a user-deﬁned subroutine.  For these 
models tying only occurs at the beginning of the simulation.  Note that we generally

recommend the AUTOMATIC_ONE_WAY_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE versions over the 
AUTOMATIC_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE versions.  
30.13.4  Alternatives to Tied Contacts 
The *CONSTRAINED keyword family provides some alternatives to tied and tiebreak 
contacts for tying nodes to nodes or to surfaces.  Some of them also include failure criteria.  
 
*CONSTRAINED_SPOTWELD, 
*CONSTRAINED_GENERALIZED_-
WELD_[SPOT, FILLET, BUTT, CROSS_FILLET, COMBINED], and *CONSTRAINED_-
BUTT_WELD provide methods of modeling welds.  They all include failure models.  
*CONSTRAINED_SPOTWELD models the spot weld with massless, rigid beams. 
 
*CONSTRAINED_NODAL_RIGID_BODY creates a rigid body from a set of 
nodes.  *CONSTRAINED_EXTRA_NODES adds extra nodes to an existing rigid body.  
*CONSTRAINED_RIGID_BODIES merges two rigid bodies together. 
 
*CONSTRAINED_TIE-BREAK ties shell edges to each other.  It creates a tie using 
two sets of nodes to deﬁne the sides of the edges and includes a ductile, strain-based 
failure model.  We intend it for modeling seams or structural joints.  In certain cases it 
may be easier to use than *CONTACT_TIED_SHELL_EDGE_TO_SURFACE. *CON-
STRAINED_TIED_NODES_FAILURE ties all the nodes in a set together.  It has failure 
based on plastic strain.  This model requires the nodes to be coincident.  *CON-
STRAINED_SHELL_TO_SOLID ties shell edges to solid elements.  However, *CON-
TACT_TIED_SHELL_EDGE_TO_SOLID is easier to use than *CONSTRAINED_-
SHELL_TO_SOLID.  
30.14  Strongly Objective Tied Contacts 
In implicit calculations, nonphysical results have been observed when some tied contact 
formulations are combined with automatic single point constraints on solid element ro-
tational degrees of freedom (AUTOSPC on *CONTROL_IMPLICIT_SOLVER).  This issue 
has motivated us to add an optional strongly objective extension to some tied contacts.  
Strongly objective means the forces and moments transform correctly under superposed 
rigid body motions in a single implicit time step.  The chosen contact types for this exten-
sion provide a universal tied contact formulation in implicit that works well in most sit-
uations.  Thus, with the available types, you should not have to ﬁgure out which interface 
is best suited for the application.  We selected the following contacts: 
*CONTACT_TIED_NODES_TO_SURFACE_CONSTRAINED_OFFSET 
*CONTACT_TIED_NODES_TO_SURFACE_OFFSET 
*CONTACT_TIED_SHELL_EDGE_TO_SURFACE_CONSTRAINED_OFFSET 
*CONTACT_TIED_SHELL_EDGE_TO_SURFACE_BEAM_OFFSET 
 

--- PAGE 689 ---
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
30-33 (Contact-Impact Algorithm) 
 
The ﬁrst two contact types do not consider rotational degrees of freedom, whereas 
the other two do.  Furthermore, the ﬁrst and third are constraint-based and the other two 
are penalty-based.  In all, these four contact types cover much of what is expected from a 
tied interface.  By setting IACC to 1 on *CONTROL_ACCURACY, LS-DYNA treats any 
of the tied contact options mentioned above (and the non-oﬀset counterparts as a side 
eﬀect, namely, *CONTACT_TIED_NODES_TO_SURFACE and *CONTACT_TIED_-
SHELL_EDGE_TO_SURFACE) with this strongly objective formulation.  
 
In addition to being strongly objective, this formulation applies rotational con-
straints consistently when and only when necessary. Thus, not only are tracked nodes with-
out rotational degrees of freedom not rotationally constrained, but also bending and 
torsional rotations are constrained to the reference segment’s rotational motion in a way 
that is physically justiﬁed.  To be more speciﬁc, the tracked node’s bending rotations 
(meaning rotations in the plane of the reference segment) are constrained to the reference 
segment rotational degrees of freedom if this happens to stem from a shell element.  Oth-
erwise, the rotations are constrained to the reference segment rotation as determined 
from its individual nodal translations.  The tracked node’s torsional rotations (that is, 
rotations with respect to the normal of the reference segment) are always constrained 
according to this latter philosophy, thus avoiding a torsional constraint to the relatively 
weak drilling mode of shells.  Thus, this tied contact formulation properly treats both 
bending and torsional rotations.  Here the tracked node’s rotational degrees of freedom 
typically come from shell or beam elements.  As a result of how rotational constraints are 
applied, it is suﬃcient to only consider: 
*CONTACT_TIED_SHELL_EDGE_TO_SURFACE_CONSTRAINED_OFFSET 
*CONTACT_TIED_SHELL_EDGE_TO_SURFACE_BEAM_OFFSET 
 
for most situations (choosing between a constraint or penalty formulation).  The other 
two “non-rotational” formulations, namely, 
*CONTACT_TIED_NODES_TO_SURFACE_CONSTRAINED_OFFSET 
*CONTACT_TIED_NODES_TO_SURFACE_OFFSET 
 
are included in the event of not wanting to constrain rotations whatsoever.

30.15  Sliding-Only Interfaces 
This option is seldom useful in structural calculations.  Its chief usefulness is for treating 
interfaces where the gaseous detonation products of a high explosive act on a solid ma-
terial.  The present algorithm, though simple, has performed satisfactorily on a number 
of problems of this latter type.  We brieﬂy outline the approach here. 
 
The method consists of ﬁve steps.  In the ﬁrst step, the mass per unit area 
(mass/area) and pressure are found at each node on the tracked surface.  Next, the con-
tact point for each reference node is found, and the tracked mass/area and tracked pres-
sure at each reference node is interpolated from the tracked surface.  In the third step, 
this pressure distribution is applied to the reference surface to update its acceleration.  In 
the fourth step, the normal component of the acceleration at each node on the reference 
surface is scaled by its 푧-factor deﬁned as the mass/area of the reference surface at the 
reference node divided by the sum of the mass/area of the tracked surface at the reference 

--- PAGE 693 ---
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
30-37 (Contact-Impact Algorithm) 
node.  The last step consists of resetting the normal acceleration and velocity components 
of all tracked nodes to ensure compatibility. 
30.16  Single Surface Contact Algorithms in LS-DYNA 
The single surface contact algorithms evolved from the surface-to-surface contact algo-
rithms and the post-contact searching follows the procedures employed for the surface-
to-surface contact.  Type 4 contact (OPTION1 = SINGLE_SURFACE for *CONTACT) 
uses the following steps where NSEG is the number of contact segments and NTN is the 
number of nodes in the interface:  
 
• Loop through the contact segments from 1 to NSEG 
◦ Compute the normal segment vectors and accumulate an area-weighted av-
erage at the nodal points to determine the normal vectors at the nodal points. 
• Loop through the tracked nodes from 1 to NTN 
◦ Check all nearest nodes, stored from the bucket sort, and locate the node 
which is nearest. 
◦ Check to see if nearest node is within a penetration tolerance determined 
during the bucket sort, if not, proceed to the end of the loop. 
◦ For shell elements, determine if the nearest node is approaching the segment 
from the positive or negative side based on the right-hand rule.  Project both 
the node and the contact segment along the nodal normal vectors to account 
for the shell thickness.   
◦ Check for interpenetrating nodes and if a node has penetrated apply a nodal 
point force that is proportional to the penetration depth. 
End of Loop 
 
Of course, several obvious limitations of the above procedure exist.  The normal 
vectors that are used to project the contact surface are meaningless for nodes along an 
intersection of two or more shell surfaces (see Figure 30.26).  In this case the normal vector 
will be arbitrarily skewed depending on the choice of the numbering of the connectivities 
of the shells in the intersecting surfaces.  Secondly, by considering the possibility of just 
one contact segment per node, metal forming problems cannot be handled within one 
contact deﬁnition.  For example, if a workpiece is constrained between a die and a blank-
holder then at least some nodal points in the workpiece must necessarily be in contact 
with two segments-one in the die and the other in the blankholder.  These two important 
limitations motivated the development of the bucket sorting algorithm described in Sec-
tion 30.9.3 and the modiﬁed single surface contact procedure, type 13 (OPTION1 = AU-
TOMATIC_SINGLE_SURFACE). 

--- PAGE 694 ---
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
LS-DYNA Theory Manual

master@e24ec890e (03/08/25)

In addition to SINGLE_SURFACE and AUTOMATIC_SINGLE_SURFACE, LS-
DYNA single surface contacts also include AIRBAG_SINGLE_SURFACE, AUTOMAT-
IC_GENERAL, and SINGLE_EDGE.  AIRBAG_SINGLE_SURFACE is based on AUTO-
MATIC_SINGLE_SURFACE with modiﬁcations speciﬁcally for airbag deployment.  AU-
TOMATIC_GENERAL is like AUTOMATIC_SINGLE_SURFACE, but it handles beam 
contact and shell edge contact diﬀerently.  *CONTACT_AUTOMATIC_GENERAL in-
cludes treatment of beam-to-beam contact in which it checks the entire length of the beam 
for penetration, not just the nodes of the beam.  For shells, it checks for penetration along 
the entire length of the exterior (unshared) shell edges.  *CONTACT_AUTOMATIC_-
GENERAL essentially adds null beams to the exterior edges of shell parts so that edge-
to-edge treatment of the shell parts is handled by virtue of contact through the automat-
ically generated null beams.  *CONTACT_SINGLE_EDGE is based on single surface con-
tact but only treats edge-to-edge contact.  It should be used with contact types that do not 
already have edge treatment.  For details about how this contact works, see Section 30.21. 
30.17  Surface-to-Surface Constraint Algorithm 
The constraint algorithm is based on the algorithm developed by Taylor and Flanagan 
[1989].  This algorithm is enabled with OPTION1 for *CONTACT set to CONSTRAINT_-
SURFACE_TO_SURFACE. This algorithm involves a two-pass symmetric approach with 
a partitioning parameter, 훽, that is set between negative and positive unity. 훽= 1 and

acts as the tracked surface and SURFB acts as the reference surface, while for 훽= −1 the

A signiﬁcant disadvantage of the constraint method relative to the penalty method 
appears if an interface node is subjected to additional constraints such as spot welds, 
constraint equations, tied interfaces, and rigid bodies.  Rigid bodies can often be used 
with this contact algorithm if their motions are prescribed as is the case in metal forming.  
For the more general cases involving rigid bodies, the above equations are not directly 
applicable since the local nodal masses of rigid body nodes are usually meaningless.  Sub-
jecting the two sides of a shell surface to this constraint algorithm also leads to erroneous 
results since an interface node cannot be constrained to move simultaneously on two mu-
tually independent surfaces.  In the latter case, the constraint technique could be used on 
one side and the penalty method on the other.   
 
The biggest advantage of the constraint algorithm is that interface nodes remain 
on or very close to the surfaces with which they are in contact.  Furthermore, elastic vi-
brations that can occur in penalty formulations are insigniﬁcant with the constraint tech-
nique.  The problem related to ﬁnding good penalty constants for the contact are totally 
avoided by the latter approach.  Having both methods available is possibly the best op-
tion of all. 
30.18  Rigid Boundaries 
The rigid boundary represents the simplest contact problem.  We, therefore, treat it sep-
arately.  In this section, we discuss both planar and geometric boundaries.  To invoke 
these boundaries, use *RIGIDWALL_PLANAR and *RIGIDWALL_GEOMETRIC. 
30.18.1  Planar Rigid Boundaries 
LS-DYNA supports ﬂat, planar boundaries of ﬁnite or inﬁnite extent.  Figure 30.28 illus-
trates a ﬁnite planar boundary.  Deﬁning a planar boundary requires specifying an out-
ward normal unit vector 퐧 with the origin of 퐧 at a corner point on the wall if the wall is 
ﬁnite or at an arbitrary point on the wall if the wall extends to inﬁnity.  The ﬁnite wall is 
rectangular with edges of length L and M.  Unit vectors l and m lie along these edges.  
 
The input for *RIGIDWALL_PLANAR includes selecting a subset of nodes, usu-
ally boundary nodes of the calculational model, that are not allowed to penetrate.  These

30.18.2  Geometric Rigid Boundaries 
The numerical treatment of geometric rigid walls is somewhat similar to that for the ﬁnite 
planar rigid walls.  The geometric rigid walls can be subjected to a prescribed transla-
tional motion along an arbitrarily oriented vector.  However, rotational motion is not 
permitted.  As the geometric surface moves and contacts the structure, external work is 
generated which is integrated and added to the overall energy balance.  In addition to the 
external work, plastic work also is generated as nodes contact the wall and assume the 
walls normal velocity at the point of contact.  Contact can occur with any of the surfaces 
that enclose the volume.  Currently, four geometric shapes are available including the 
rectangular prism, the cylinder, ﬂat surface, and sphere.  These are shown in Figure 30.29.

ever rerun, LS-DYNA can read the VDA input directly from the binary ﬁle, thereby sig-
niﬁcantly reducing startup time.  The die in this example is made up of several surfaces 
and faces from two diﬀerent VDA ﬁles.  This format of input enables combining any

number of faces, surfaces, and groups from any number of VDA ﬁles to deﬁne a single

The contact algorithm works as follows.  For the sake of simplicity, we will refer 
to one point as being tracked by a single part.  Again, this part will in general be made 
up of several VDA surfaces and faces.  First, the distance from the tracked point to each 
VDA surface is computed and stored.  For the surface nearest to the tracked point, several 
other parameters are stored, such as the surface coordinates of the nearest point on the 
surface.  This information is updated during each time step of the calculation.  For the 
nearest surface, the new nearest point on the surface is calculated.  For all other surfaces, 
the distance the tracked point moves is subtracted from the distance to the surface.  These 
updates continually give a lower bound on the actual distance to each VDA surface.  
When this lower bound drops below the thickness of the point being tracked, the actual 
distance to the surface is recalculated.  Actually, if the nearest surface is further away 
from the tracked point than some distance, the nearest point on the surface is not tracked 
at all until the tracked point comes close to some surface.  These precautions result in the 
distance from the tracked point to a surface having to be totally recomputed every few 
hundred timesteps, in exchange for not having to continually track the point on each sur-
face. 
 
To track the point on the nearest surface, a 2D form of Newton's method is used.  
The vector function to be solved speciﬁes that the displacement vector from the surface 
to the tracked point should be parallel to the surface normal vector.  The surface tangent 
vectors are computed with respect to each of the two surface patch parameters, and the 
dot product taken with the displacement vector.  See Figure 30.30 and Equation (1.108).

in it).  Iteration continues until the maximum number of allowed iterations is reached, or 
a convergence tolerance is met.  The convergence tolerance (as measured in the surface 
patch parameters) varies from patch to patch, and is based on the size and shape of the 
patch.  The convergence criterion is set for a patch to ensure that the actual surface point 
has converged (in the spatial parameters 푥, 푦, and 푧) to some tolerance.

30.20  Simulated Draw Beads 
The implementation of draw beads is based on elastic-plastic interface springs and nodes-
to-surface contact.  The area of the blank under the draw bead is taken as the reference 
surface.  The draw bead is deﬁned by a consecutive list of nodes that lie along the draw 
bead.  For straight draw beads only two nodes need to be deﬁned, but for curved beads 
suﬃcient nodes must be used to deﬁne the curvature.  The draw bead line is discretized 
into points that become the tracked nodes to the reference surface.  The spacing of the 
points is determined by LS-DYNA such that several points lie within each reference seg-
ment.  This is illustrated in Figure 30.32.  The dense distribution of point leads to a smooth 
draw bead force distribution which helps avoid exciting the zero energy (hourglass) 
modes within the shell elements in the workpiece.  A three-dimensional bucket search is 
used for the contact searching to locate each point within a segment of the reference sur-
face. 
 
The nodes deﬁning the draw beads can be attached to rigid bodies by using the 
extra nodes for rigid body input option.  When deﬁning draw beads, care should be taken 
to limit the number of elements that are used in the reference surface deﬁnition.  If the 
entire blank is speciﬁed, the CPU cost increases signiﬁcantly, and the memory require-
ments can become enormous.  An automated draw bead box, which is deﬁned by speci-
fying the part ID for the workpiece and the node set ID for the draw bead, is available.  
The automated box option allows LS-DYNA to determine the box dimensions.  The size 
of this box is based on the extent of the blank and the largest element in the workpiece as 
shown if Figure 30.33.   
 
The input for the draw beads requires a load curve giving the force due to the 
bending and unbending of the blank as it moves through the draw bead.  The load curve

30.21  Edge-to-Edge Contact 
Edge-to-edge contact can be important in some simulations.  For example, if a fan blade 
breaks away from the hub in a jet turbine, contact with the trailing blade will likely be 
along the edges of the blades.  Edge-to-edge contact requires special treatment since the 
nodal points do not make contact with the reference segment, which is the basis of con-
ventional contact treatments.  Currently, only *CONTACT_AUTOMATIC_GENERAL, 
*CONTACT_SINGLE_EDGE, all contacts using the segment-to-segment (SOFT = 2) for-
mulation with certain values of DEPTH, and all automatic Mortar contacts possess edge-
to-edge capabilities.  
 
Other than *CONTACT_AUTOMATIC_GENERAL_INTERIOR and segment-to-
segment (SOFT = 2) contacts, the previously mentioned contacts only treat contact be-
tween exterior edges.  *CONTACT_AUTOMATIC_GENERAL_INTERIOR and the seg-
ment-to-segment (SOFT = 2) contacts additionally support edge contact for interior 
(meshline) edges.  Additionally, all the previously mentioned contacts other than seg-
ment-to-segment (SOFT = 2) contact only support edge contact for shell elements.  The 
segment-to-segment (SOFT = 2) contact supports edge contact for shells, thick shells, and 
solids. 
 
*CONTACT_SINGLE_EDGE is a older contact based on the single surface formu-
lation.  It has an identical input to the single surface formulation.  However, it only con-
siders contact between edges and does not treat nodes to surface contact.  When the 
surface is deﬁned by part ID, edge determination is automatic.  It is also possible to use a 
manual deﬁnition by listing line segments.  This contact only considers edge-to-edge con-
tact of the type illustrated in Figure 30.37.  Here, the tangent vectors to the plane of the 
shell and normal to the edge must point to each other for contact to be considered. 
Figure 30.36.  Contact between edges requires a special treatment since the 
nodes do not make contact.

30.22  Beam-to-Beam Contact 
In beam-to-beam contact, the contact surface is assumed to be the surface of a cylinder as 
shown in Figure 30.38.  The diameter of the contact cylinder is set equal to the square root 
of the area of the smallest rectangle that contains the cross section to avoid tracking the 
orientation of the beam within the contact algorithm.  Contact is found by ﬁnding the 
intersection point between nearby beam elements and checking to see if their outer sur-
faces overlap as seen in Figure 30.39.  If the surfaces overlap, the contact force is computed 
and applied to the nodal points of the interacting beam elements.

30.23  Mortar Contact 
Mortar contact was initially implemented as a forming contact intended for stamping 
analysis.  It has since become a general-purpose contact algorithm for implicit time inte-
gration.  Mortar contact is available for automatic single and surface-to-surface contacts.  
It features proper edge treatment, beam contact, and optional features, including tied, 
tiebreak, and interference.  Contact is often the one feature that hinders implicit perfor-
mance.  Thus, the LS-DYNA message ﬁles contain substantial information on penetra-
tions to facilitate debugging of Mortar contacts.  
 
Mortar contact is a penalty-based segment-to-segment contact with ﬁnite-element-
consistent coupling between the non-matching discretizations of the two sliding surfaces.  
The implementation is based on Puso and Laursen [2004a,b].  This consistency, together 
with a diﬀerentiable penalty function for penetrating and sliding segments, enforces the 
continuity and (relative) smoothness in contact forces that is appealing when running 
implicit analyses.  The algorithm primarily focuses on accuracy and robustness.  The cal-
culations associated with this aim make it expensive enough to be recommended for im-
plicit analysis ﬁrst and foremost.  
 
The implementation includes numerous details that cannot be explained without 
making the presentation incomprehensible.  The intention here is to summarize the gen-
eral concepts of the theory behind the implementation and draw upon this to make gen-
eral recommendations on usage. 
30.23.1  Kinematics 
Mortar contact is theoretically treated as a generalized ﬁnite element where each element 
in this context consists of a pair of contact segments.  Mortar contact models friction with 
a standard Coulomb friction law.  Each of the two segments inherits its isoparametric 
representation from the underlying ﬁnite element formulation, so the coordinates for the 
tracked and reference segments can be written as:

translational forces on the nodes along the edge.  For beams, nodal rotations are involved 
in the kinematics, and frictional torques are accounted for but in a diﬀerent way. 
30.23.4  Treatment of beams, sharp solid edges, and shell edges 
Automatic Mortar contacts support contact with the lateral surface and end tips of beams 
as well as edges of shell elements and sharp edges of solids.  The concept of sharp, solid 
edges will be deﬁned below.  In this case, the abovementioned theory is applied to 
dummy segments corresponding to a faceted representation of the beam lateral surface 
and the edges of the solid and shell elements, as indicated in Figure 30.41. For a beam 
element, the contact surface is represented by 14 faceted segments encapsulating a 
cylinder with the same length and volume as the beam element.  This implies that all 
beam elements are assumed to have a circular cross-section for the contact.  The edges of 
the shell element surface are identiﬁed assuming the contact deﬁnition (tracked or 
reference) consists of the entire physical component (metal sheet).  We, therefore, 
recommend deﬁning the contacts using part or part sets.  Otherwise, false edges may be 
created in the interior of the component.  
 
An edge contact element is created for shells by extruding the shell edge by a 
distance corresponding to the shell thickness with appropriate adjustments for irregular 
geometries.  As mentioned above, the kinematics that create these edge segments do not 
account for their numerical representation.  Hence, Mortar contact does not assemble the 

--- PAGE 714 ---
Contact-Impact Algorithm 
LS-DYNA Theory Manual 
30-58 (Contact-Impact Algorithm) 
master@e24ec890e (03/08/25) 
corresponding forces in a ﬁnite-element-consistent manner.  The shell edge treatment is 
to be seen as a simpliﬁed treatment that incorporates contact resistance for these 
geometries, which is probably okay in most practical situations.  For beam elements, 
however, rotational degrees of freedom are included consistently, thus causing beam 
elements to rotate with respect to their axes when tangential friction forces are applied to 
the lateral surface.  
 
A sharp, solid edge is detected when the angle 휃 between the normals of two 
adjacent contact segments is larger than 휋/3. In this case, the edge is smoothed by adding 
four segments between the two nodes common to the two contact segments while at the 
same time adjusting the size of the two main contact segments.  The eﬀect is a rounded 
representation of the edge and a smoother contact response.  See Figure 30.41. The size of 
the smoothing is at most 5% of the size of the smallest of the two contact segments, so the 
eﬀect is reduced with mesh reﬁnement.  Because the contact area of these edge segments 
may be small, the stiﬀness of the contact for those segments is scaled by the factor 훽=
√3cot (휋−휃
2 ), where 휃 is the initial angle between the main segments’ normal vectors.  This 
scale factor is applied to both the tracked and reference sides, meaning that if two right-
angled

2 ) = 9. Whether this is suﬃcient to handle most common 
situations is currently unknown.  Hence, this design decision is subject to change in the 
future.  If a contact segment has two sharp edges with a common node, a segment is 
created at the location of that node to account for contact with the corner of the solid 
element geometry.  The stiﬀness scale factor for a corner node is the average of the scale 
factors for the connected edges.  
 
The motivation behind solid edge smoothing is twofold.  First, it adds penetration 
resistance between a solid edge/corner and other geometries.  Second, it aids in 
establishing a physical contact state when solid elements slide oﬀ sharp geometrical 
objects.  More speciﬁcally, it eliminates the ambiguity of which contact segments are in 
contact and presumably prevents sudden spikes in the contact force.  This is also 
illustrated in Figure 30.41. 
 
It is important to stress that automatic Mortar contact surfaces are always on the 
outer geometry for both the tracked and reference sides.  In other words, contact does not 
occur on the midsurface of shells. Figure 30.42 illustrates a typical modeling problem that 
results in extremely large contact stress unless the IGNORE ﬂag is appropriately used.  
 
Forming contact is treated diﬀerently than automatic contact.  Shell edge and beam 
contact are not supported.  Additionally, any shell reference surface must be rigid with its 
segment normal vectors oriented towards the tracked side of the contact.  Furthermore, 
the contact occurs at the midsurface on the reference side at the midsurface and on the 
outer geometry for the tracked side.  The segment orientation of the (deformable) 
reference side is arbitrary, but, if it consists of shell elements, contact can only occur on 
one side for a given contact deﬁnition.  For instance, the contact between the tool and 
blank and the contact between the die and blank must be deﬁned using two diﬀerent 
contact interface because these contacts typically occur on diﬀerent sides of the blank.

30.23.5  Characteristic Length and Contact Release 
The characteristic lengths of the tracked and reference sides are denoted by 푑푐
푡 and 푑푐
푟, 
respectively.  They are important in Mortar contact because they aﬀect the contact 
stiﬀness.  They also determine the maximum allowed penetration, 푑max, between two 
arbitrary segments.  To be more speciﬁc, two segments cannot penetrate more than 95% 
of the average characteristic lengths.  Penetrations larger than that are not detected.  In 
mathematical terms this can be stated as: 
푑max = 0.95 푑푐
푡+ 푑푐
푟
2
(30.120)
 
Figure 30.43 illustrates the eﬀect of maximum penetration by giving the contact 
stress as a function of relative penetration.  Increasing the stiﬀness parameter, SFSA, can 
minimize the risk of releasing contacts but may lead to worse convergence in implicit 
analysis.  To stiﬀen the contact for large penetrations without aﬀecting moderate 
penetrations, use the parameter IGAP. Figure 30.43 illustrates the aﬀect of this parameter.  
IGAP can be used if the contact pressure is locally very high.  This discussion highlights 
that Mortar contact has no “stick” option for improving implicit convergence.  IGAP may 
lead to worse convergence characteristics but rules out sticky behavior and 
underreportting of contact forces.  
 
The characteristic length for shells is the shell thickness.  For solids it is the smallest 
element size in the part to which the segment belongs.  The latter may lead to 
unrealistically high or low contact stiﬀness, or it may result in a too small maximum 
penetration depth, depending on the mesh.  Setting PENMAX to the characteristic length 
may alleviate these issues.  PENMAX should correspond to some physical member size 
in the model and/or adjust the contact stiﬀness, depending on the issue.

30.23.6  Output for Debugging Implicit Models 
In implicit analysis it is almost inevitable to run into convergence problems, especially 
when contacts are involved.  To obtain detailed information on penetration distance and 
potential contact release (meaning penetration becomes too large for the contact to be 
detected in subsequent steps), set MINFO = 1 on *CONTROL_OUTPUT. This option 
causes the LS-DYNA to provide information on the largest penetration, both absolute and 
relative, in the message ﬁles after each converged step, including a warning if penetration 
is close to being released.  It also reports the elements with largest penetrations, making 
it easy to locate critical areas of the model in LS-PrePost.  Contact release should be 
avoided.  Otherwise, results may be useless. 
 
Additionally, poor convergence can be due to a too stiﬀ contact.  Because the stiﬀ-
ness for a Mortar contact segment pair only depends on the tracked segment, we recom-
mend putting weak parts on the tracked side.  If a steel part is in contact with rubber, for 
instance, the rubber part should be on the tracked side in the contact deﬁnition.  Turning 
on D3ITCTL on *CONTROL_IMPLICIT_SOLUTION and RESPLT on *DATABASE_EX-
TENT_BINARY aid in ﬁnding isolated areas in the model with poor convergence.  Not 
rarely this is due to contacts.
